title: How do you generate your game assets without it looking like AI slop?
author: SnooChocolates6293

comments.author: ChadSexman

comments.author: meowyih

comments.author: GigaTerra
comments.body:
You put that work into it. That is it, either you embrace AI and the time it saves, side effect is it's style gets into your work, or you do the work that normally takes an team of artist yourself, and get something unique. 

However it is linear, so you can do part of the work, and use AI partially, and then only get partial part of the AI look.

comments.author: SolrayCultist
comments.body:
I suck at this so just letting you know I'm in the same boat as you. But what I've been experimenting with is drawing as much as I can of at the very least, the basic gist. And sort of using that as a framework for the AI to build on. Then I describe the purpose of a thing. I'm not certain and this might aound strange, but I feel if I get my agent excited about the lore behind things, it feels more inspired? Mixed results though. Not great and not reliable yet. For context, these are pixel art assets. 

Thought I'd mention it, in case it helped, or maybe get some additional tips myself.

comments.author: PsychronicGames
comments.body:
With my own engine, what I did was I created a system that generates the assets with code, and then keep iterating until you get a consistent result, once built, it's technically not AI, but you might have used the AI to code the thing that builds the thing. This is my engine, still working on it though:

RPG Reactor:  
[https://psychronic.itch.io/rpg-reactor](https://psychronic.itch.io/rpg-reactor)

Source Code:  
[https://github.com/Psychronic-Games/RPGReactor](https://github.com/Psychronic-Games/RPGReactor)

It's still a work in progress but keeps getting better, and it's not like a "slot machine" with each new generation, although I have to keep iterating it to make it better, but it's getting there! The idea is that it's a hybrid engine that is AI friendly but also all human-editable too.

AI can one-shot 80% of it, but that last 20% is the hardest part and often needs that personal touch, etc.

comments.author: Frederik77
comments.body: It probably always will, unless you hand the generated art to an actual artist as inspiration or for cleaning it up. You could also try prompting for assets in a specifically defined unique art style to still give your game an interesting look,so that players will think more about the art direction and actual look than about whether it looks ai-generated. The less generic your prompt is, the less generic the result will probably be.

comments.author: random_boss
comments.body: I use free and paid human made assets

comments.author: JohnJamesGutib
comments.body: I think, for code, images, audio, and even music, with enough effort and skill on your part, you can make it pretty polished and *not* sloppy at all. For 3D models and 3D animation however, I think it's practically impossible for now. The effort you would have to put in to make 3D models and 3D animation not sloppy is *so much* that you're literally better off just making the entire thing from scratch yourself. I've found this to be true even if your artstyle is low poly and low res pixelated - the output is still horrendously sloppy.

comments.author: GlobalCurry
comments.body: For 2D art I do what most of my traditional artist friends showed me to do, which is create a style reference board and pass it in as part of the prompt for art.

replies.author: GlobalCurry
replies.body: The only downside is that I'm not an artist so most of my results still look deriving while my artist friends create a few boards of their own style and can generate stuff that looks unique and passes as hand made.

comments.author: goblingamescompany
comments.body:
Claude Desktop (code) with Replicate connector setup. Use Claude to create an art guide: colors, times, theme, style, etc. use Claude to also ensure you have a selected art style: 2d, 3d, pixel, etc.

Give a reference angle of media, art, whatever - not to copy but to help inform.

Generate a first swing, get it right, scale from there 

I can ask Claude now to Regen my whole art set pretty easily 

Here's my current game with that workflow: https://store.steampowered.com/app/5376910/The_Last_God/?beta=1

comments.author: daddy_reloaded
comments.body:
Currently the only way I reach good enough 3d assets is to model part separately and assemble them manually (could do automatically but it's still faster manually today). Any Opus/astra workflow (three.js, python+blender) starting from good 2d concept will perform quite well if the part is small enough.
And the tripod/meshy tools is still useful for some assets (like characters), but I still generate them in parts and manually modified them with blender.

I sometimes buy assets and rework them in blender.

Still looking for the optimised way, but it seems that it clearly depends on the game.

comments.body: i use tripo. i let claude make a prompt and then fine tune it, make a reference image first and when i like it, i use the smartmesh image -> model and the results are pretty decent. it just takes a bit of practice to get the desired results.

comments.author: Templeshooter
comments.body: I was generating icons for spells and items in game and qwen image kept putting realistic characters in them, which gave away the images as slop, I then modified the negative prompt to exclude realistic anatomy and it started producing mannequin looking figures, which read much better when scaled down and look way less "sloppy"
